choices: A rhythm of a slow opening, a developing middle and a rapid close
questions.explain: It's a principle of tempo and intensity: jo, ha, kyū.

questions.q: An actor's single entrance, a scene and a whole evening's program are all shaped slow, building, fast. Which of Zeami's ideas is at work?
choices: That jo-ha-kyū applies at every scale
questions.explain: Zeami treated jo-ha-kyū as nested: each part of the whole has its own jo, ha and kyū.

questions.q: Which part of jo-ha-kyū is the longest?
questions.explain: In Zeami's ideal five-section play, ha takes three of the five sections.

choices: The living effect on the audience: freshness and the unexpected
questions.explain: The flower is the effect a performance produces, tied closely to novelty.

questions.q: A feature writer opens with a burst of drama and then lets the piece slacken over a long ending. What would jo-ha-kyū suggest?
choices: Keep the energetic top and cut the ending
Open more calmly, deepen through the middle, and quicken toward a brisk close
Put the most important facts first
questions.explain: Jo-ha-kyū gives the audience time to settle, then builds and accelerates, ending before they tire.

questions.q: What does yūgen mean in Zeami's usage?
choices: Refined, graceful beauty with a sense of hidden depth
questions.explain: Originally 'dark' or 'deep', it came to mean elegant beauty that suggests more than it shows.

questions.q: How is jo-ha-kyū fundamentally different from McKee's five-part design?
choices: It concerns tempo and intensity, not a protagonist's struggle toward a goal
questions.explain: Zeami's principle is about how energy moves through a performance, not about conflict.

ideas: Every unit of a performance, from a single gesture to a full day's program, should open slowly, deepen, and close quickly.
Success on stage is a flower: fresh, admired because it fades, and stronger when the audience can't see how it's done.
The highest quality of performance is a graceful beauty that hints at depths it never shows.
